Tata Trusts challenges Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as Tata Sons chairman

Tata Trusts declares N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons chairman invalid, citing AoA violations and lack of affirmative director support.

ANI

20 September, 2026 05:39 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran at unveiling of Tata Avinya concept car in Mumbai on 29 April, 2022 | Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as Chairman of Tata Sons was not validly passed at the company’s September 17 board meeting as the mandatory support of Tata Trusts’ nominee directors was not secured, Tata Trusts said on Sunday.

According to Tata Trusts, Tata Sons’ Articles of Association (AoA) require the affirmative support of a majority of directors nominated by Tata Trusts, which hold approximately 66 per cent of the company. With two Tata Trusts nominees on the board, both directors would have to support the resolution for the separate condition under the AoA to be met.

One of the two nominees voted against the resolution on September 17, meaning the required affirmative support was not available, the Trusts said.

Show Full Article

The Trusts further said the Chairman’s casting vote cannot be used to overcome the failure of this condition, as such a vote is available only in case of equality of votes at the overall board level and does not apply to the requirement concerning Tata Trusts’ nominee directors.

“There was no paralysis and there was no deadlock. The Board put a question, and the AoA answered it in the negative,” the Trusts said.

The Trusts also referred to the Supreme Court proceedings arising from the removal of former Tata Sons chairman Cyrus Mistry, arguing that Tata Sons had previously defended the affirmative voting rights of Trusts’ nominee directors under Articles 104B and 121.

The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal had held these rights to be oppressive, but the Supreme Court accepted Tata Sons’ position and set aside that finding, according to the release.

The Trusts said Tata Sons therefore could not now disregard protections that it had previously defended before the Supreme Court.

The Tata Trusts also rejected the argument that listing Tata Sons would be necessary to strengthen its corporate governance, pointing to existing provisions covering independent directors, audit and nomination committees, related-party transactions, retirement of directors by rotation and insider trading.

The Trusts said these governance standards had been adopted voluntarily by Tata Sons before the current issue arose. (ANI)

Trump’s Greenland deal changes little. His bullying can change US-Denmark ties

As Donald Trump ended his confrontation over Greenland, European leaders were remembering the enormous risks taken as the Cold War began to descend on their borders.

Praveen Swami

20 September, 2026 05:05 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US President Donald Trump | Daniel Heuer | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

E ight metres below the endless darkness of the Arctic winter, there were hot showers, flush toilets and a cafeteria serving double portions of steak and ice cream. The 21 tunnels cut into the ice sheet of northern Greenland in 1959 were to have grown into a 1,25,000 square-kilometre secret city , housing hundreds of nuclear missiles aimed at the Soviet Union. Even as winds exceeding 200 kilometres per hour lashed the surface and temperatures fell below minus 50°C, the portable PM2A nuclear reactor powering the ice city ensured it was always summer inside.

“Life inside the mile-thick glacier is not too different from that in many small US, Canadian or British towns,” a visitor recorded : Even if those towns were annihilated in a nuclear war, civilisation would live on under the ice.

However, t here was one small catch: The Social Democratic coalition that had won Denmark’s 1957 election had vowed, in writing, not to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its soil. The decision followed a threat made by Soviet Prime Minister Nikolai Bulganin earlier that year: “For countries the size of Denmark, the granting to foreign powers of the possibility of establishing bases would, in the event of the outbreak of an atomic war, be synonymous with suicide.”

Show Full Article

Last week, as US President Donald Trump ended his months-long confrontation over Greenland by gloating over what he claims to be a historic new agreement, European leaders were remembering the enormous risks taken as the Cold War began to descend on their borders.

Fearing that its North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) allies might break ranks over the deployment of nuclear weapons in Europe, the State Department ordered its ambassador to Denmark to meet Prime Minister Hans Christian Hansen.

Even though he’d heard about “the possible storing of supplies of munition of a special kind in the defence areas in Greenland,” Hansen responded, the Denmark government had not been presented with concrete plans or asked about its attitudes. The equipment the United States chose to store on its bases was, in any case, “permitted entry into Greenland free of inspection.”

As long as he was told nothing, Hansen was saying, he was willing to allow nuclear missiles to be stationed at American bases in Greenland, and risk Soviet wrath.

New words, old wars The text of the new Greenland agreement hasn’t been released, but officials have said it gives America “permanent access, basing and overflights rights,” as well as the “unilateral power to build additional military structures.” The agreement is also thought to contain provisions barring adversaries of the US —like China or Russia—from deploying troops in Greenland, or making investments in strategic sectors. Trump claimed the agreement allowed the US to address its security concerns at “no cost to the United States.”

All of this would be a significant victory—if it hadn’t already been won in 1951. For little more than a few moments of social media bragging, Trump has taken a hammer to the trust built over generations.

The Defence of Greenland Treaty of 1951 gave the US the right to control airspace and anchorage over designated defence areas. The kingdom also ceded its right to enforce its laws against, and to collect taxes from, American military personnel. The Treaty was to stay in effect as long as the North Atlantic Treaty, which had no date of expiry. Laws subjecting foreign investments in Denmark to security screening were put in place in 2021. Greenland began working on a similar legal framework three years later .

From as early as November 1945—eight weeks after the end of the Second World War—American war planners began preparing the first drafts of their nuclear war doctrine , as part of a thoroughgoing study of Soviet military capabilities. These early efforts had crystallised by 1946, when a plan drawn up for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, recommending expansion of America’s nuclear arsenal, concluded that nuclear weapons could “nullify any nation’s military effort and demolish its social and economic structures.”

America’s nuclear arsenal was small—growing from nine warheads in 1945 to 56 in 1948—but the country’s leadership believed it offered a means to offset Western deficits in numbers. Greenland and Iceland were critical elements of nuclear deterrence. Few aircraft could fly transatlantic, and refuelling bases were needed along polar routes. Those routes also enabled surveillance of the Soviet submarine fleet.

The February 1948 coup in Czechoslovakia, followed by the blockade of West Berlin, persuaded former US President Harry Truman that the Soviets had to be confronted . That summer, he d i spatched B-29 bombers to Europe—a declaration of willingness to use nuclear weapons to defend America’s allies.

Europeans were not universally persuaded of the wisdom of the emerging doctrine of nuclear deterrence. The US believed that stationing nuclear weapons on the territory of NATO partners would strengthen deterrence. To both Denmark and Norway, though, there seemed a real risk that nuclear weapons stationed on their soil might invite attack. A complex series of negotiations followed, carving out an exception in Greenland: The language of Danish sovereignty would not apply to American defence zones on the island.

Also read: Trump threatened to redraw the map. Greenland deal shows the limits of his disruption

The Wholesale e mpire The Arctic Eden had, in fact, been bid for long before the Cold War: the sea, a determined buyer’s brochure recorded , was awash with “whale, walrus, seal, and shark, cod, ivory-cod, salmon, salmon-trout, and herring; foxes, wolf, reindeer, bear, hare, myriads of birds, including the king duck, eider duck, dorskin, petrel, gull, brent, burgo-master, goose, killiwoke, lolard, and sea swallow.”

Like most marketing material, the text had raced just a little ahead of reality: “Killiwoke,” likely a misspelling of kiviak, was a dish made of fermented seabirds, not a kind of wildlife. There was, it was true, enough coal to power a merchant fleet and summer routes across the Bering Strait from Europe to East Asia.

Long before Trump and rare-earth metals lobbyists began pushing the idea, US Secretary of State William Seward—the force behind the purchase of Alaska for $7.2 million—decided Iceland and Greenland should be added to the American empire.

To Seward and other American imperialists, their case was unassailable —and not because of the wildlife. American naval power would be able to flank what an 1868 g overnment publication called British America—the territory that had become Canada the previous year. Like Trump, Seward believed that control of the territory off Canada’s eastern coast would “greatly increase her inducements, peacefully and cheerfully, to become a part of the American Union.”

Few in America, though, were keen to buy. The problem was that Americans didn’t want their taxes spent buying what the newspapers were starting to call a Polar Bear Garden, an Ice-Box, or, even more unkindly, Seward’s Folly. The discovery of gold and oil in Alaska was still decades away.

The idea didn’t disappear. In 1910, America’s ambassador to Denmark, Maurice Egan, proposed a territorial swap , which would have restored the European principality of Schleswig-Holstein to Denmark, in return for a cluster of Philippine islands America would have given to Germany. Then, in 1940, Germany invaded Denmark. The US responded by occupying Greenland, and asserting that the island was covered by the Monroe Doctrine—the American declaration prohibiting any foreign strategic presence in the Western Hemisphere.

Enemies had changed, more than once, through the 20th century—but geography hadn’t. The question was how leaders of the transatlantic alliance could reconcile conflicting aims and values to protect their shared interests.

Also read: The 2026 midterms will test the political foundations of American power abroad

Friends and lovers Geography is changing, though—and that change underpins the growing strategic significance of Greenland. The Arctic sea routes will be ice-free throughout the year before the middle of this century, opening up fast routes between ports in China, Russia and America’s western seaboard. The ice-city built in 1959 had to be abandoned within two decades because the enormous pressure exerted by the shifting ice sheet crushed the tunnels.

The melting of the ice sheets over Greenland, though, will make mining for rare-earth metals and hydrocarbons commercially viable. The question is: Was it really necessary for the US to assert sovereignty over Greenland to secure its interests and regulate the new regional order?

The story of the transatlantic relationship offers us a simple answer. Throughout the Cold War, the Danish leadership went to extraordinary lengths to protect and nurture their relationship with NATO and the US.

Following the crash of a B-52 bomber off Thule in 1968—which led to a cloud of radioactive material from its four nuclear bombs being spewed over the ice-bound port—the US agreed to demands for Greenland to become a nuclear-free zone. This was, in part, because nuclear submarines and ballistic missiles had made conventional bombers irrelevant. For their part, Danish authorities agreed to language that would allow nuclear weapons back on Greenland in some circumstances.

Leaders in both Washington and Copenhagen understood that their alliance was anchored in one core interest: the need to defend themselves against the Soviet Union. To do so, however, they had to make complex compromises, sometimes even resorting to lies and deceit. The solutions, though, emerged from hard-won trust, not braggadocio or bullying.

Praveen Swami is a Contributing Editor at ThePrint. His X handle is @praveenswami. Views are personal.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

Diana’s brother compares media treatment of Harry, Meghan to late princess’ ordeal

Reuters

20 September, 2026 02:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

LONDON, Sept 20 (Reuters) – The media’s treatment of Prince Harry and his wife Meghan is on a par with that faced by his mother Diana, the late princess’ brother said in an interview published on Sunday, warning that lessons needed to be learned from that period.

Diana died aged 36 in a 1997 Paris car crash as photographers pursued her on motorbikes, sparking an outpouring of grief and a reckoning over whether the media bore some responsibility for her death after splashing details of her life across front pages for years.

“If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant,” Diana’s brother, Earl Charles Spencer, told the BBC.

Show Full Article

“And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example.

“I’m not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life.”

Harry, Diana’s youngest son, and Meghan, cited the impact of what they called a toxic media on their lives before they quit royal duties and moved to the United States in 2020.

They also sued much of the British tabloid press – with varying degrees of success – before they moved back to Britain in August.

Spencer has made headlines around the world in the last week after his book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister”, was serialised in the Daily Mail, accusing her former husband, the now King Charles, of sounding “giddily elated” in the hours after her death.

The palace hit back by saying the king “is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”.

The publication of the book and the return of Harry and Meghan to Britain are another challenge for the king, who is still undergoing treatment for cancer.

Diana’s family accused the royals of showing a lack of support or care towards the late princess before her death, a charge that was repeated by Harry, who is now largely estranged from the rest of the royal family.

(Reporting by Kate Holton;Editing by Helen Popper)

North Korea fires ballistic missile off east coast, Seoul says

Reuters

20 September, 2026 02:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

SEOUL, Sept 20 (Reuters) – North Korea launched a ballistic missile off its eastern coast on Sunday, its second test in roughly a week and days after Pyongyang accused the US of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the test firing from the Wonsan area around 3 p.m. (0600 GMT), identifying the weapon as a ballistic missile. Japan’s defence ministry also said it appeared to be a ballistic missile.

Japanese public broadcaster NHK said the projectile had come down outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.

Show Full Article

South Korea’s National Security Council condemned the short-range missile launch, which follows a test on September 12. The council urged Pyongyang to immediately cease missile activity, warning that the test directly violated UN Security Council resolutions.

On Saturday, North Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang’s nuclear programme.

Pyongyang last week also condemned a US-led naval drill which included South Korea and Japan and which ran from August 29 to September 10 near Guam.

North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for “ever-worsening” tensions on the Korean Peninsula and vowed no change in the country’s course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

(Reporting by Cynthia Kim and Heejin Kim in Seoul and Junko Fujita in Tokyo; Editing by William Mallard and Michael Perry)
